inputs: Tribute, booty, workshop supplies, and multiple craft traditions
making: Workshops around Fort Shalmaneser's courtyards repaired and stored military equipment
coordination: A royal review palace, magazines, barracks, and a palace overseer joined crafts to an army administration
distribution: Inspection, storage, repair, and issue through the royal military complex
visible_anchor: One clay docket records 36,242 bows inspected; separate excavated finds include iron spearheads and armour
interpretation: Scale came from coordinating people records stores and repair across many crafts—not from one very large furnace.
limits: The bow docket is not iron output; the surviving depot is not an empire-wide inventory; excavated objects were filtered by looting destruction survival excavation and selective publication.

inputs: Local bog or lake ore, charcoal, clay, stone, and food resources
making: Several small smelting units; at Sangis blooms moved to a habitation-site smithing area
coordination: Chemical and spatial evidence supports multiple households as stakeholders around a centrally placed smithing site
distribution: A local exchange network connected dispersed furnaces to primary and secondary smithing
visible_anchor: Sangis 842 lay under 500 m from Sangis 730; the habitation site preserved at least three smithing hearths
interpretation: Complex production did not require a state or city: households could coordinate skill raw materials and exchange locally.
limits: The household network is a published inference from chemistry and spatial patterning; the sites do not identify named producers ownership rules annual output or a universal hunter-gatherer model.

inputs: Ore and fuel landscapes linked to farming settlements and unenclosed production sites
making: Iron production was not confined to the largest enclosed settlements
coordination: Salač interprets oppida primarily as distribution nodes rather than dominant production centres
distribution: Exchange linked dispersed producers settlements and oppida
visible_anchor: The published regional synthesis explicitly separates where goods were made from where they were distributed
interpretation: Urban-looking nodes could scale circulation without monopolizing manufacture or proving centralized political command.
limits: This is an interpretive regional model rather than a complete production census; oppida varied; distribution importance does not demonstrate free markets private ownership or weak politics everywhere.

architecture: state monopoly with a frontier gap
inputs: Iron made by casting and forging in several technological traditions across the empire
making: The Han state monopolized iron and salt after 119 BCE; Lingnan evidence includes local bloomery smelting but many imported objects
coordination: Central authority regulated production and trade, yet the Han Shu records no official iron office in Lingnan
distribution: Frontier demand was supplied substantially through movement from other regions rather than one local state works
visible_anchor: 119 BCE monopoly; no tieguan recorded for Lingnan; sampled objects preserve cast iron, wrought iron, and steel
interpretation: A central policy could scale production while still leaving regional gaps that trade and mixed technologies had to bridge.
limits: The project reports preliminary analyses; absence of a recorded tieguan is not proof of no officials or no local production; imported origin remains an argued interpretation rather than a complete provenance census.

inputs: Ore, charcoal, technical ceramics, and a changing city-edge production geography
making: Multiple slag-mound areas and permanent furnace workshops accumulated in distinct early and late phases
coordination: Long-lived production clustered around Meroe and Hamadab, but archaeology does not yet identify one stable management regime
distribution: Production shifted among areas east, north, and south of the Royal City and at Hamadab
visible_anchor: 97 radiocarbon dates from nine slag mounds; production potentially spanned more than one thousand years
interpretation: Durability could come from a production landscape that was rebuilt and relocated across political change—not one timeless royal factory.
limits: Slag volume is not metal output; broad radiocarbon ranges and complex deposition limit phase precision; proximity to a royal city does not by itself prove palace ownership monopoly or centralized labour.
